S01.label: The pubs, its convenient and simpler
S01.description: It is common as it is easy to decide to go there and you can drink, get food, chat and sometimes watch sports
S01.quote: Yeah, so for me it's usually the pub, to be honest. There's a few we rotate between — got a couple near where I work, and then there's one closer to home that's a bit more relaxed, you know? Cheaper pints, less loud. That's where we tend to end up most weekends.

S01.label: Someones flat
S01.description: Sometimes someone else flat to cook or chat, as an alternative to the traditional pub option
S01.quote: But I'd say since covid or whatever, me and my mates have actually started mixing it up a bit more than we used to. Like, we'll do a brewery or go to someone's flat to cook something, watch a film. It's not always the pub anymore

S01.label: Nights at the usual pub have less interaction
S01.description: Getting tired of the same plan to hang out with friends as sometimes you dont even talk
S01.quote: I think it's just... the pub is so easy to default to that you don't really question it. But you're saying something real there about actually being present. Because you're right, half the time you're checking your phone, someone's got the game on, you're not really talking about anything deep or memorable.

S01.label: Essential to not overthink what to do with your friends
S01.description: Men find it annoying to plan outings too much; they prefer not to make a big deal out of it.
S01.quote: I suppose we do end up just sitting in the same spot, same as Ibrahim's saying, but I don't think we've got the option to switch it up as much even if we wanted to. And honestly, for us it kind of works because everyone knows where you'll be. You don't need to plan it to death — you just go down there Friday night and your mates are there or they'll be there soon enough.

S02.label: A plant-based diet requires extra effort (eg. time, cooking meals, avilable options, etc.)
S02.description: Changing one's diet is considered a hassle because of the effort it would require and because the environment does not make that transition any easier
S02.quote:
Right, so here's the thing — this isn't just about whether your mates will judge you. That's one bit of it, yeah, but there's actual practical stuff that gets in the way.

Like, work lunches. I grab something at lunch most days, and options around here are... they're not great if you're actually trying to do plant-based properly. It's not like I'm being picky — there's just not much there. It's either a salad or nothing, and sometimes not even that. So you'd have to start bringing stuff from home, which means planning, which means extra effort. And that's every single day, not just when you're out with mates.

S02.label: Family pressure to keep status quo
S02.description: The family might question these decisions, either because they see them as an attack on the way they cook at home or because they feel other family members are being forced to adopt a new diet or because groceries for the household should change or its disrupting family habits and dynamics
S02.quote:
Because if I went vegan and it was just about meal planning and bringing stuff to work, that'd be fine. My Thursday lads wouldn't care, I could sort my lunches. But it's the family thing that's different. It's not just Sunday dinner with my mum — it's that if I made that choice, suddenly I'm saying something about how she does things, or what she cares about. And that matters in a way that your mates don't, you know?

And actually, now that I'm thinking about the kids thing — because a couple of my lads are going to be parents — it's even more complicated. Because once you've got a kid, your choices aren't just about you anymore. If you decided to go vegan, you're also deciding that for your kid, at least initially. And that's when people — family, other parents, whoever — they're going to have proper opinions about it. It's not just "oh, he's made a choice," it's "he's forcing his choices on his kid."

S02.label: The pressure to keep status quo will fade eventually, a matter of patience
S02.description: Eventually, the people who initially questioned your decision will get used to your new habits or diet
S02.quote:
Like, with my Friday group — different from the Thursday lads — one of them started going to the gym seriously, proper diet changes, all of that. And his mum was the same way at first, you know? She'd make comments about him being fussy or whatever. But he just... kept doing it. Didn't make a big thing out of it, didn't argue with her, just quietly got on with his choice. And eventually — and I'm talking months, not weeks — it just became normal. She stopped commenting. It became the thing he does.

So I'm not saying the wear-down isn't real. It is. But I think there's a middle ground between "willpower solves everything" and "it's permanently exhausting." It's maybe just... accepting that there's going to be some awkwardness for a bit, and then it settles down once people realize you're serious and you're not going to be talked out of it.

S03.label: The pubs, its convenient and simpler
S03.description: It is common as it is easy to decide to go there and you can drink, get food, chat and sometimes watch sports
S03.quote: The pub, really. That's where most of it happens. You can sit down, have a drink, chat without anyone expecting you to be doing anything else. It's low-key. I see the lads maybe once a week or so, and the pub's just the default. It's comfortable, you know? You don't have to plan much — you just meet up, grab a pint, and that's that. Some of us might grab food there too, depending on the pub, but honestly it's more about just being able to sit and talk without the background of life getting in the way.

S03.label: Age leads you to pay more attention to food choices
S03.description: Getting older make you think more of how meals are prepared or where do they come from, not in a strict way more like trying to have better food
S03.quote:
Thing is, I think I've become more aware of that over the years without really trying to. When you're younger you just eat whatever, don't think about it much. But now, I don't know, you start to actually taste the difference between something that's been looked after and something that's just been... done. And once you've noticed it, you can't unknow it, can you? You go back somewhere and you think, yeah, this is fine, but it's not the same.

I'm not going to pretend I'm checking where everything comes from or anything like that — I still do my shop at Tesco like everyone else. But when you do go to someone who's put the work in, whether that's the local butcher or a pub that's actually bothered, it just... it makes sense. You get what you're paying for. And that matters to me now more than it used to, if I'm being honest.

S04.label: It would be neccesary that plant-based diets would be as common or normal as meat-based diet
S04.description: If it would be as common as a meat-based diet, it would not be questioned so much or at least it would not feel like choosing the less safe choice
S04.quote:
But right now, I think I'm aware enough of what Amir's saying about it being a safe choice — like, eating meat is the thing you don't have to explain. So it'd have to get to a point where not eating meat was equally... unremarkable? Where nobody would clock it or read something into it. That's the practical bit that's actually about the social stuff, I suppose.

And I mean, I'm not sat here saying I want to go vegetarian anyway, so this is a bit hypothetical. But if I'm being honest about what would need to change, it'd probably be that. The normalcy bit. Because the actual cooking and eating side of it — that's easy enough. It's the other thing that's the blocker.

S05.label: Don't plan meals in advance neither overthinking what to cook
S05.description: It is preferred to be practical at the moment of choosing what to eat, don't give second thoughts to it
S05.quote: Ah, well, for me, I don't, I don't really think too, too hard about it. It’ll just be, uh, whatever's sort of in the freezer or fridge. I don't plan, plan in detail, uh, in advance or go to the supermarket specifically thinking about what days to buy. I’ll just buy various things, um, I like the look of when I'm in the supermarket and then, as and when decide to eat them. So it's really no specific, um, plan with me, just whatever I fancy on that particular day.

S05.label: Time is a key factor and depends on work schedules, so we don't plan much
S05.description: It depends on the schedule for the week, but we try to be practical—sometimes we order takeout, sometimes we eat out, and sometimes we cook something simple.
S05.quote:
Yeah, I think it depends what I'm doing. So like, obviously I'm working in, I'm actually on site in the office. I do normally work hybrid. So I usually go in one or two days a week out of the four days that I work. Um, I work in Manchester and live on the whirl. So for me, um, tonight, you know, I've planned for the partner that I will just bung a couple of pizzas in, um, because it's a, you know, it takes 10 minutes. Then obviously we can actually spend a bit of the time in the evening with our kid.
Last night because I was at home working, um, I had actually planned out meals. So I'll, I'll try and have a rough plan based around what the schedule for the week is, but um equally I can get home tonight and go, you know, I can't even be assed cooking a pizza. Let's order a takeaway because, you know, hour long train journey.
So it, it yeah, there's no real plan, um, that we stick to, but I do try to have a bit of a, an idea. But yeah, it's fluid.

S05.label: A practical alternative is to prepare meals that will last for several days and that you know everyone will enjoy
S05.description: It's essential to use your time efficiently, and you don't want to spend too much time preparing meals or learning new recipes
S05.quote: Yeah, we've got a slow cooker, actually. I was gonna say we've got six people in the house. Um, so, we've kind of got a load of meals that we know everybody, everybody'll eat. And then we tend to batch cook them. I actually work from home most of the time, so I can kind of cook something in the afternoon. But it's really a case of just making these big vats of food that'll last us for a couple of days and just going round with the stuff we know that everyone will eat. So, um, yeah. Yeah, it's not the most adventurous.

S05.label: It's a blessing when your partner cooks—it takes the burden of worrying about meals off your shoulders, and you just eat whatever's there.
S05.description: You don't have to worry about what to eat if you're not the one in charge of preparing meals at home—it's much easier
S05.quote: Um, well, I'm unemployed at the moment, as is my partner. Um, I'm quite fortunate that she's, um, half Italian and loves to cook. Um, so I kind of don't decide, I'll be honest. Um, so she tends, it's a bit lazy, I must admit, but she tends to, um, make the lunches and dinners and enjoys doing so. I mean, I'll chip in where I can. Um, but as I say, I tend not to decide. Um, we have similar tastes, so that's, that's fine. Um, yeah, but it's, um, it's kind of the decision is taken out of my hands. Um, it wasn't when I was working, but it kind of is at the moment, but I'm, I'm happy to, to go with that at the moment.

S06.label: Price and taste of plant-based are the main barrier
S06.description: Plant-based food should taste very similar to what we're used to and not be too expensive for us to consider making the switch
S06.quote: For me again, it's down to the price and taste. If it was, if it was cheap and tasted the same, then I'd be perfectly happy to buy it. If it was more expensive, probably less so.

S06.label: Health improvement reason from consuming plant-based
S06.description: If it had health benefits and given that the person engages in physical activity, it would be interesting
S06.quote: Um, and then if that, yeah, the one that would still really resonate with me is, is just around the, the health, overall fitness. [unintelligible] stock, creaking in my later cricketing years. If I could extend my health, um, further to be able to keep playing for a few more years. So I think something like that would be appealing to me. But I, personally I think, um, protein is a good thing. And meat is a good way of consuming it.

S06.label: Protein is better in meat-based diet
S06.description: It is believed that switching to a plant-based diet would result in an inadequate intake of protein.
S06.quote: But I, personally I think, um, protein is a good thing. And meat is a good way of consuming it. It's great that it tastes really nice. And I probably know I should eat a little bit less red meat so, sits sits with me. Um, I think it's those health messages.

S06.label: Ingredients in plant-based foods aren't healthier
S06.description: It has been reported that plant-based foods contain fats and sugars that make them unhealthy, so there is considered to be no reason to make them an alternative
S06.quote: But from what I hear and what I read a lot of these plant based and substitute meals are actually, they're loaded with with with sugars and salts and fats that don't actually make them any healthier for me. So again, maybe if they kind of got a little bit more, uh, adept at producing stuff that that is healthy, a real truthful, um, healthy alternative, then maybe so.

S01.label: The pub as the default, low-effort social space
S01.description: Meeting at the pub is highly favored because it is convenient, allows people to come and go flexibly, and requires very little planning or coordination.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: And everyone knows where they're going without having to plan it to death.

evidence.speaker: Participant 2
evidence.quote: Still the easiest option though when you just want to turn up without planning anything.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: The pub you can just rock up, have a couple, leave when you want.

S01.label: Shared activities foster deeper connection and memorable experiences
S01.description: Participating in active, organized experiences like cooking together at home encourages meaningful conversations and creates stronger, more lasting memories than passive drinking routines.

evidence.speaker: Participant 2
evidence.quote: You're talking properly, making food, eating together. Versus the pub where you're just... drinking and watching whoever's match is on.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: Those stick with you more than just another pint night, don't they?

S01.label: Alternative activities require too much effort and commitment
S01.description: Organizing active hangouts like group cooking is seen as demanding because it requires upfront planning, longer-term time commitments, and active participation.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: And I'll go along with it, but... I don't know, it feels like more effort sometimes? Like you've got to commit to being there for longer, help with the cooking or whatever.

S01.label: Rural social options are limited by geography and logistics
S01.description: In rural areas, a lack of diverse venues means socializing inevitably revolves around the single local pub, as alternative urban-style activities are logistically difficult.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: So it's not really a choice between the pub and doing something at someone's place the same way. Like, if you want to see your mates it's usually the pub, because that's where people go.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: It's just... logistics are a bit different when you're not in a city with loads of options, you know?

S02.label: Logistical and financial barriers to plant-based eating
S02.description: Daily logistical friction like limited work lunch options, required meal planning, and higher costs pose major practical barriers to adopting a plant-based diet.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: Like, work lunches. I grab something at lunch most days, and options around here are... they're not great if you're actually trying to do plant-based properly.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: And honestly, there's the cost thing too. Plant-based options out, or proper versions of stuff — it's more expensive usually.

S02.label: Dietary changes as a perceived judgment on family
S02.description: Choosing to eat plant-based can be perceived by family members as a personal criticism of their cooking, traditions, and values.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: She'd take it as a criticism of what she cooks. And my older relatives would definitely have opinions.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: It's not just Sunday dinner with my mum — it's that if I made that choice, suddenly I'm saying something about how she does things, or what she cares about.

S02.label: Relational wear-down as an unsustainable barrier
S02.description: The ongoing, low-level emotional tension with family over dietary choices creates a mental wear-down that makes maintaining a plant-based diet practically unsustainable.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: Sometimes it's the relational stuff that makes the practical stuff unsustainable.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: Because like Bilal said, you can have all the logistics sorted, but if every time you're at your mum's there's this low-level awkwardness or you feel like you're being difficult, it just... wears you down.

S02.label: Normalization through quiet persistence
S02.description: Family and social friction from a dietary shift is temporary and can eventually settle into a new normal if the person quietly persists with their choice over time.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: It's maybe just... accepting that there's going to be some awkwardness for a bit, and then it settles down once people realize you're serious and you're not going to be talked out of it.

S02.label: Parental choices and external judgment
S02.description: Adopting a plant-based diet for children is highly complicated because others view it as forcing choices on a child, which invites significant social and family judgment.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: Because once you've got a kid, your choices aren't just about you anymore. If you decided to go vegan, you're also deciding that for your kid, at least initially. And that's when people — family, other parents, whoever — they're going to have proper opinions about it. It's not just "oh, he's made a choice," it's "he's forcing his choices on his kid."

S02.label: The buffering effect of collective shifts
S02.description: Undergoing a major lifestyle or dietary transition alongside peers significantly reduces the social friction and tension compared to doing it completely alone.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: It's about whether you've got people around you who are shifting at the same time, or whether you're genuinely on your own with it.

S02.label: Lack of conscious intention as a barrier to change
S02.description: The primary barrier to changing one's diet for some is simply a lack of a compelling reason to change and an absence of active reflection on what they eat.

evidence.speaker: Participant 2
evidence.quote: Because I haven't really... thought about it enough to want to change, you know? It's not like I've got a barrier I'm fighting against. I just don't have a reason to do it yet.

S03.label: The pub as a low-stress default space for connection
S03.description: The pub serves as a comfortable, default location where male friends can relax, sit down, and have meaningful conversations free from the pressures and interruptions of daily life.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: The pub, really. That's where most of it happens. You can sit down, have a drink, chat without anyone expecting you to be doing anything else.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: so the pub becomes a bit of a release, just having that space where you can talk without interruption.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: You just want to sit down and actually talk to someone without the phone going off or someone needing something from you.

S03.label: Shift from youthful indulgence to quieter social experiences with age
S03.description: As they get older, men's socializing shifts away from drinking to excess or trying to impress others, focusing instead on quieter, more conversational gatherings.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: I mean, when we were younger it was more about going out and getting hammered, but now it's quieter. You want to actually sit and have a conversation, especially at forty-five.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: It's the same for me at forty-seven — you're not trying to prove anything anymore, are you?

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: at forty you're not trying to impress anyone anymore. You just want to sit down with people you know and not have to think too hard about it.

S03.label: Value of quality pub food in enhancing the social experience
S03.description: While food is not the primary reason for visiting the pub, well-sourced and properly cooked food significantly enhances the enjoyment of the evening and encourages them to stay longer.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: it makes the whole experience better if it's done well. You're more inclined to stay longer, have another pint if the food's good and you're not sitting there regretting what you ate.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: ordered a steak, and it was just... you could tell someone cared about where it came from. Not expensive or anything, just decent quality beef cooked right. Made a real difference to the evening.

S03.label: Growing awareness of food quality paired with a practical attitude
S03.description: With age comes a permanent awareness and appreciation of better-quality food, though this is balanced with a practical, non-obsessive attitude toward everyday sourcing and shopping.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: And once you've noticed it, you can't unknow it, can you? You go back somewhere and you think, yeah, this is fine, but it's not the same.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: I'm not going to pretend I'm checking where everything comes from or anything like that — I still do my shop at Tesco like everyone else.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: But like you say, Andrew, I'm not going out of my way to source everything perfectly or anything daft like that. It's just... if I'm going to eat something, might as well be something decent if it's there.

S04.label: Social normalcy as the primary barrier
S04.description: Adopting a plant-based diet is blocked more by the social discomfort of doing something different or feeling 'weird' than by the practical difficulties of cooking and eating without meat.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: Because the actual cooking and eating side of it — that's easy enough. It's the other thing that's the blocker.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: Yeah, that's the thing though, isn't it? What Isaiah's saying — the normalcy bit is the blocker.

S04.label: Unconscious collective maintenance of normalcy
S04.description: The normalcy of eating meat is kept in place through a circular dynamic where individuals make the 'safe' choice and avoid questioning or discussing it, thereby reinforcing it for others.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: We're all kind of maintaining it, aren't we? By not questioning it, by making the safe choice without thinking about it too much.

S04.label: Conscious choice requires personal responsibility
S04.description: Once individuals become aware of the social patterns surrounding meat-eating, opting for an alternative means making a conscious 'statement' that must be defended, which is harder than simply following the effortless default.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: Because once you start questioning it, once you make it a choice instead of just the default, you're the one who has to own that. You can't just... not think about it anymore.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: And that means if you actually wanted to do something different, you'd have to own it consciously. You couldn't just eat meat without thinking about it anymore because you'd know what you were doing.

S04.label: Meat-eating as an unexamined default rather than a social choice
S04.description: Some individuals do not feel they are actively maintaining social norms or making symbolic choices about masculinity when eating meat; it is simply what they eat without prior thought.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: I just eat meat, it's what I do, and I haven't been walking around aware that I'm choosing it for some performance reason or whatever.

S05.label: Spontaneous and unplanned meal selection
S05.description: Meal choices are often made spontaneously based on immediate desire or what is currently available in the kitchen, rather than through structured planning.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: I don't plan, plan in detail, uh, in advance or go to the supermarket specifically thinking about what days to buy. I’ll just buy various things, um, I like the look of when I'm in the supermarket and then, as and when decide to eat them.

S05.label: Work schedules and time constraints dictate meal planning
S05.description: Meal choices and preparation are heavily shaped by busy work schedules, long commutes, and limited energy at the end of the day.

evidence.speaker: Participant 2
evidence.quote: So I'll, I'll try and have a rough plan based around what the schedule for the week is, but um equally I can get home tonight and go, you know, I can't even be assed cooking a pizza. Let's order a takeaway because, you know, hour long train journey.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: Yeah, I'd say as well, time is quite a big factor in terms of, um, what you eat in some ways, because like, not so much a problem for now, because I'm a teacher, but during like school term time, staff meeting night, Wednesday, it's always long. So I don't really want to be spending ages cooking.

S05.label: Working from home enables greater cooking flexibility
S05.description: Working from home provides individuals with the time and opportunity to prepare or cook meals during the afternoon.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: perhaps if anyone works from home, they might have more chances to put something in the oven whilst they're still working and, and, and have that cooking away.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: I actually work from home most of the time, so I can kind of cook something in the afternoon.

S05.label: Large household meals revolve around batch-cooked, universally liked food
S05.description: Cooking for a large family involves making large quantities of simple, familiar meals that are guaranteed to satisfy everyone's tastes.

evidence.speaker: Participant 4
evidence.quote: we've kind of got a load of meals that we know everybody, everybody'll eat. And then we tend to batch cook them.

S05.label: Deferring meal choices to a cooking partner
S05.description: Some individuals do not have to make meal decisions because their partner handles and enjoys the cooking entirely.

evidence.speaker: Participant 5
evidence.quote: she tends to, um, make the lunches and dinners and enjoys doing so. I mean, I'll chip in where I can. Um, but as I say, I tend not to decide.

S06.label: Price and taste parity
S06.description: Plant-based foods would become appealing if they were as cheap and tasted as good as meat options.

evidence.speaker: Participant 2
evidence.quote: For me again, it's down to the price and taste. If it was, if it was cheap and tasted the same, then I'd be perfectly happy to buy it.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: it really would come down to price if it was significantly cheaper.

S06.label: Masculinity is not a barrier
S06.description: The idea that eating plant-based foods is unmanly is outdated, and men do not judge each other for choosing them.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: certainly within my social group, the men aspect of it is just a, just a, we wouldn't even consider it being kind of unmanly.

S06.label: Health benefits and physical fitness
S06.description: Clear health benefits, such as extending one's active years and fitness, make plant-based foods more appealing.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: the one that would still really resonate with me is, is just around the, the health, overall fitness.

S06.label: Unhealthy additives in plant-based substitutes
S06.description: Many processed meat substitutes are unappealing because they are high in sugars, salts, fats, and artificial additives.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: from what I hear and what I read a lot of these plant based and substitute meals are actually, they're loaded with with with sugars and salts and fats that don't actually make them any healthier for me.

evidence.speaker: Participant 2
evidence.quote: it's probably that that gives it its, its nicer taste, it makes it, makes it taste nice or makes it taste like what it’s trying to simulate.

S06.label: The phrase "plant-based" is loaded
S06.description: The term "plant-based" feels accusatory and loaded, whereas encouraging people to eat more fruit and vegetables is a more positive message.

evidence.speaker: Participant 3
evidence.quote: plant based just feels a really loaded, um, really loaded phrase. And actually encouraging people to eat more fruit and veg is actually a better message.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: plant based does sound, you're right, it does sound accusatory.

S06.label: Sensory replication of meat
S06.description: Processed substitutes must successfully mimic the exact taste and texture of the meat they are trying to replace to be acceptable.

evidence.speaker: Participant 1
evidence.quote: Now if they came up with some sort of amazing plant based bacon that that to me tasted and had the texture of bacon, um, then maybe that would, that would steer me down that route
